title: Number That Survives Two Flips
statement:
Flipping a non-negative integer means writing its decimal digits in reverse order and reading the result as a number, so any leading zeros disappear. For example, flipping 3200 gives 0023, which is 23.

Given num, flip it, then flip the result again. Return true if you end up with num again, otherwise false.

examples.why: 3200 → 23 → 32. The trailing zeros were lost on the first flip.
0 → 0 → 0. Zero has no trailing zero to lose, even though it ends in the digit 0.

hints: Try a few numbers by hand. When does the first flip lose information?
A flip only drops zeros that end up in front. Those were the zeros at the end of num.
num survives exactly when it has no trailing zero, with one exception: 0 itself.

explain.intuition:
Reversing digits is lossless except for one thing: zeros at the end of num move to the front and vanish. Every other digit comes back in its place after the second flip. So the only numbers that change are those ending in 0.

The exception is 0: it is a single digit that stays 0 after any number of flips. So the answer is num === 0 || num % 10 !== 0.
steps: Otherwise return whether the last digit, num % 10, is non-zero.
pitfalls: Only checking whether num is a palindrome. 418 is not a palindrome but still comes back.

solutions.title: Simulate both flips
solutions.idea: Reverse the digits arithmetically twice and compare.

solutions.title: Check the last digit
solutions.idea: Only trailing zeros get lost, and 0 itself is safe.

followups: How many integers in [0, n] survive two flips? Answer without a loop.
The number is given as a string with possible leading zeros. What changes?
